newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: Bahrain forecasts smaller deficit in 97/98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Bahrain forecasts smaller deficit in 97/98 budget.

text.p: Small oil producer Bahrain on Tuesday announced its two-year 1997/98 budget, forecasting a lower deficit and higher revenue, bolstered by a projected increase in oil earnings.

In a decree issued by the Emir Sheikh Isa bin Sulman al-Khalifa, Bahrain forecast a deficit of 150 million dinars ($398 million) compared to the projected 236 million dinar spending-income gap in the 1995/96 budget.
"The oil income in the new budget has achieved a dramatic increase based on changes in world oil prices," Finance and National Economy Minister Ibrahim Abdel-Karim said.
The decree, carried by the Gulf News Agency (GNA), projected spending in the next two years of 1.395 billion dinars with income seen at 1.245 billion dinars.
It did not say what oil price the budget was based on.
The 1995/96 budget had forecast spending of 1.29 billion and income of 1.05 billion dinars.

Bahrain is a small and independent oil producer with around 40,000 barrels per day (bpd) from its own fields. It also began receiving in April the entire production of 140,000 bpd from an offshore oil field it shared with Saudi Arabia.
The island, the Gulf's main financial and banking centre, also imports 200,000 bpd from Saudi Arabia for refining.
The budget projected 1997 income at 615 million dinars and spending at 690 million dinars, while 1998 income was forecast at 630 million dinars and expenditure at 705 million dinars.
Abdel-Karim said Bahrain plans to spend 1.15 billion dinars on development projects in the next four years.

"The government has allocated 1.150 billion dinars for vital development projects in an investment programme for the next four years," he said. It was not immediately clear how Bahrain would finance the projects.

Sheikh Isa last week altered the law to allow Abdel-Karim to issue treasury and development bonds worth not more than 600 million dinars at any one time. Bahrain issues treasury bills weekly and longer maturity bonds from time to time.
Bankers say they believe the amendment allows Abdel-Karim to double the outstanding amount of issued bills and bonds.

Abdel-Karim said Bahrain would implement several projects in the fields of electricity and water, transport, roads, causeways, housing, health and education as well as building a new sea port to meet increasing economic activities.
The new projects include a power and water plant to produce 250 megawatts of electricity and 30 million gallons a day of water and a port which is expected to be ready by 2000.
A new hospital and several new schools will also be built.
Abdel-Karim said the investment opportunities would help find more jobs for its citizens.
Bahrain has also allocated 7.5 million dinars for training in the next two years, up 22 percent on 1996, Abdel-Karim said.
